alt: A chain: a pupil in a low GCSE set is entered for the foundation tier, which caps the highest grade available. Below, arguments for and against streaming, setting and mixed ability teaching.
caption: Through tiered entry, a set placement can directly limit the grade a pupil can achieve.

alt: A four-step cycle: a teacher labels a pupil as not academic; the teacher gives easier work and less praise; the pupil sees themselves through the label and loses effort; achievement falls, which seems to confirm the label.
caption: A label becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy only when it comes true.

alt: Concentric circles with the teacher’s ideal pupil at the centre. Middle-class pupils sit close to the centre; working-class pupils sit further out and are more likely to be seen as badly behaved. Below, Rosenthal and Jacobson’s experiment as bonus evidence that expectations can change outcomes.
caption: Teachers judged pupils against an ideal that was closest to middle-class pupils.

alt: Two cohorts. In the banded cohort, middle-class pupils were more often placed in band 1 and prepared for higher-status exams, while band 2 was steered to lower-status courses and developed anti-school attitudes: polarisation. In the mixed ability cohort polarisation was less marked, but teachers’ expectations still favoured middle-class pupils.
caption: Banding worked as an institutional label that shaped pupils’ attitudes and exams.

alt: The lads formed a counter school culture, felt superior to teachers and to conformist ear’oles, and aimed to have a laff. Rejecting school suited them to male-dominated manual work, easy to get in the 1970s. Below, Ball shows the institution shaping pupils while Willis shows pupils actively resisting.
caption: Willis shows pupils actively choosing resistance, which still led to manual work.
